To be enamored means to be filled with a deep, powerful feeling of love, admiration, or fascination — toward a person, a thing, or even an idea. It goes far beyond simply liking something. When you are enamored, you are captivated. You can't stop thinking about it. It holds a special, almost magical place in your heart or mind.

Think of it as the feeling when something or someone grabs hold of you so strongly that you are pulled toward it with warmth and excitement.

The word works in two related but distinct situations:

1. Romantic love
This is the more traditional use. Being enamored with a person means you are deeply, intensely attracted to them — you are smitten, enchanted, in love. It carries a sense of being under a spell.

He was completely enamored with her — he thought about her all day and smiled every time her name came up.

2. Strong admiration or fascination (non-romantic)
This is just as common and important. You can be enamored with a place, a hobby, an idea, a book, a city, a sport — anything. It means you find it deeply appealing, you are drawn to it, and you enjoy or admire it greatly.

She became enamored with painting after her first art class — she bought brushes that same evening.
The tourists were enamored with the city's old streets and colorful markets.
He has always been enamored with the idea of traveling the world alone.

This is important: enamored is not a mild word. It sits well above "interested" or "fond of." Here is a rough ladder to show you where it stands:

  • Slightly interested → fond of → in love with / fascinated by → enamored → obsessed

Enamored sits near the top. It suggests a strong, warm, genuine feeling — but it is not yet obsessive or unhealthy. It is deeply positive and enthusiastic.

Here is a nuance that makes the word richer: when someone is enamored, they often see the object of their admiration through rose-colored glasses. They may overlook its flaws or imperfections because they are so charmed by it.

He was so enamored with the old house that he ignored all the cracks in the walls and the leaking roof.

This slight sense of being charmed to the point of not seeing things clearly is built into the word's feeling, even if it isn't always stated directly.

"Enamored" is almost always followed by with or of. Both are correct, though enamored with is more common in American English, and enamored of is more traditional and slightly more formal.

  • She was enamored with the novel.
  • He was enamored of her wit and intelligence.

You will almost never see "enamored" standing alone without one of these prepositions following it.
The Negative Form — and Why It Matters

One highly useful way the word appears is in the negative: not enamored with/of.

When used this way, it is a polite, understated way of saying you dislike something or are unimpressed by it. This is common in formal or professional speech.

The manager was not enamored with the new proposal. (= she didn't like it at all)
I have to say, I'm not particularly enamored with this plan. (= I think this is a poor idea)

Notice how saying "not enamored with" sounds more measured and sophisticated than simply saying "I hate this" or "I don't like this." It is a refined way of expressing disapproval.
The Register: When Do People Use This Word?

"Enamored" is a slightly formal and literary word. You are more likely to encounter it in:

  • Written English (novels, articles, essays)
  • Formal or professional speech
  • Situations where someone wants to sound expressive or eloquent

In everyday casual conversation, people are more likely to say "I'm obsessed with," "I'm in love with," "I'm fascinated by," or simply "I really love" — but all of those can often be replaced by "enamored" when you want a more refined tone.

AspectDetail

Enamored means deeply captivated — by a person (romantically) or by anything else (a place, idea, hobby, work of art) through powerful admiration and fascination. It is stronger than "liking" something. It carries a warm, enchanted quality, sometimes with a hint of being so charmed that you overlook flaws. It is paired with with or of, and in its negative form (not enamored with), it becomes a refined way to express dislike or disapproval. It is a slightly formal word, most at home in writing or thoughtful speech.

Once you know this word, you will start noticing it everywhere — and you may even find yourself becoming a little enamored with it.
